item.title: Venerable Udaya: “I have come with a question — To the meditator, sitting dustless, Duty done, without defilements, Who has reached the far shore —…
item.description:
Venerable Udaya:
“I have come with a question —
To the meditator, sitting dustless,
Duty done, without defilements,
Who has reached the far shore —
Speak the knowledge of liberation,
The breaking of ignorance.”

The Blessed One replied to Udaya:
“Abandon desire for sensual pleasures,
Both sorrow and grief;
Abandon sloth and torpor,
And prevent remorse.

Knowledge of liberation, I say,
Is the breaking of ignorance —
Purified by equanimity and mindfulness,
With reflection leading the way.”

Venerable Udaya:
“What binds the world?
What is its range?
By abandoning what is Nibbāna called?”

The Blessed One:
“The world is bound by delight;
Directed thought is its range.
By abandoning craving,
Nibbāna is called.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 5.14

item.title: “Fear, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Suffering, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Disease, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A…
item.description:
“Fear, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Suffering, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Disease, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A boil, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Clinging, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A bog, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. And why, monks, is fear a synonym for sensual pleasures? Monks, infatuated by sensual desire, bound by sensual desire, one is not free from fear in this very life, nor free from fear in the future. Therefore, fear is a synonym for sensual pleasures.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.23

item.title: “Monks, while Prince Vipassī was going to the pleasure garden, he saw a sick person, suffering, gravely ill, wallowing in his own urine and feces,…
item.description:
“Monks, while Prince Vipassī was going to the pleasure garden, he saw a sick person, suffering, gravely ill, wallowing in his own urine and feces, needing others to lift him, needing others to support him. Seeing this, the prince asked the charioteer: ‘Good man, what has this person done that his eyes are not like those of others, his voice not like others?’ ‘Your Highness, that is called a sick person.’ ‘Good man, why is he called a sick person?’ ‘Your Highness, he is called a sick person because he has not recovered from his illness.’ ‘Good man, then am I subject to sickness, not having fallen sick yet?’ ‘Your Highness, you and I as well — all of us are subject to sickness, even though we have not fallen sick yet.’ ‘Good man, then this visit to the pleasure garden is enough. Drive back to the palace.’ ‘Yes, Your Highness.’ Monks, the charioteer, obeying the prince, drove back to the palace. Monks, Prince Vipassī returned to the palace, suffering, grieving, and thought: ‘Shameful indeed is this birth! And anyone who is born must also age, must also be sick!’”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 14 – Mahāpadānasutta

item.title: Elder Nun Sumedhā: Even if there were seventeen treasures, Filling the ten directions completely, Sensual desires are never satisfied — One dies, still unsatisfied. Sensual…
item.description:
Elder Nun Sumedhā:

Even if there were seventeen treasures,
Filling the ten directions completely,
Sensual desires are never satisfied —
One dies, still unsatisfied.

Sensual desires are like swords and spears,
Sensual desires are like a snake’s head,
Like a blazing torch,
Like a smooth-gnawed bone.

Sensual desires are not permanent,
Nor are they everlasting —
Much suffering, a great poison,
Like a red-hot iron ball —
The source of misfortune,
Resulting in suffering.

Sensual desires are like a fruit tree,
Like a piece of meat — trouble,
Like a dream, like a illusion —
Sensual desires are like borrowed goods.

Sensual desires are like swords, like stakes,
Disease and boils,
Misfortune and agitation —
Like a pit of glowing embers —
The source of misfortune,
Fear and destruction.

Fools, for a long time,
Weep in this wandering continuation.
From beginningless time until now,
They weep at being subject to death,
Weep for slain brothers,
Weep for being slain themselves.

Remember from beginningless time —
Tears, milk, and blood
Flow in saṃsāra,
Without ever stopping.
Remember the accumulation of bones
Of beings wandering on.

Remember the four oceans
Filled with tears, milk, and blood —
Remember the bones of one lifetime,
As high as Vepulla.

Remember from beginningless time —
Not enough to make
The whole Jambudīpa
As a heap of mustard seeds
Of mothers and fathers in saṃsāra.

Remember from beginningless time —
Grasses, trees, branches, leaves —
Not enough to contain
A four-fingered pot
For the fathers in saṃsāra.

Remember the image
Of the blind turtle in the eastern sea,
Poking its head into
The hole of a floating yoke —
To illustrate
How hard it is to be human.

From: Therīgāthā 16.1
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, desire and lust for the eye is a defilement of the mind. Desire and lust for the ear … for the nose … for…
item.description:
“Monks, desire and lust for the eye is a defilement of the mind. Desire and lust for the ear … for the nose … for the tongue … for the body … for the mind is a defilement of the mind. When a monk has abandoned these defilements in regard to these six sense bases, his mind inclines to renunciation. Having been fully saturated with renunciation, his mind becomes wieldy and he directly knows the things to be fully known.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 27.1

item.title: “Monks, if anyone would develop these four foundations of mindfulness for just seven days, one of two fruits could be expected: either final knowledge here…
item.description:
“Monks, if anyone would develop these four foundations of mindfulness for just seven days, one of two fruits could be expected: either final knowledge here and now, or if there remains a trace of clinging, the state of non-return. Monks, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, for the realization of Nibbāna – namely, the Four Foundations of Mindfulness.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 10 – Satipaṭṭhānasutta

item.title: “Suppose, Rādha, young boys or girls are playing with sandcastles. As long as their desire, lust, love, thirst, passion, and craving for those sandcastles are…
item.description:
“Suppose, Rādha, young boys or girls are playing with sandcastles. As long as their desire, lust, love, thirst, passion, and craving for those sandcastles are not fully abandoned, they still cling to them, delight in them, treasure them, and are attached to them. But when their desire, lust, love, thirst, passion, and craving for those sandcastles are fully abandoned, then they smash them, scatter them, demolish them with their hands and feet and no longer play with them. So too, Rādha, you should smash, scatter, demolish form and not play with it, being intent on the destruction of craving for form. The destruction of craving, Rādha, is Nibbāna.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.2

item.title: “And, monks, shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, this body of the wise person is generated. That ignorance the wise person abandons. That craving…
item.description:
“And, monks, shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, this body of the wise person is generated. That ignorance the wise person abandons. That craving the wise person destroys. Why is that? Monks, the wise person lives the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body, after death, the wise person does not go to another body. Not going to another body, he is freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is freed from suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.19
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Furthermore, Sāriputta, a monk should reflect: ‘Have I abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure?’ Sāriputta, if a monk, on reflection, knows: ‘I have not…
item.description:
“Furthermore, Sāriputta, a monk should reflect: ‘Have I abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure?’ Sāriputta, if a monk, on reflection, knows: ‘I have not yet abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure,’ then he should strive to abandon them. But if, on reflection, he knows: ‘I have abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure,’ then he should dwell with joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 151 – Piṇḍapātapārisuddhisutta

item.title: Thus he abides contemplating the body as a body internally; or he abides contemplating the body as a body externally; or he abides contemplating the…
item.description:
Thus he abides contemplating the body as a body internally; or he abides contemplating the body as a body externally; or he abides contemplating the body as a body both internally and externally. Or he abides contemplating the nature of arising in the body; or he abides contemplating the nature of passing away in the body; or he abides contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the body. ‘There is a body,’ he establishes mindfulness just enough for knowledge and mindfulness. And he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world. Thus, monks, a monk abides contemplating the body as a body.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 22 – Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta
